text: You've seen the definitions in isolation across the last three lessons — now the real skill: given a problem you've never seen before, correctly place it, and defend that placement. This lab is worked practice, not new theory.

Use these four questions, in order. Can a classical computer solve it directly in polynomial time? If yes, it's in P, and automatically in every larger class too. If not, can a proposed answer be verified quickly? If yes, it's at least in NP, and NP-complete if every other NP problem reduces to it. Is there a known quantum algorithm that beats the best classical one — and if so, is that speedup exponential, Shor-style, or quadratic, Grover-style? And if no quantum algorithm offers an advantage, say so explicitly — that's a real, correct, final answer for most problems.

Two worked examples show how differently this can go. Factoring a 2048-bit RSA modulus: no efficient classical algorithm is known, the best is the sub-exponential General Number Field Sieve, but Shor's algorithm solves it in polynomial time on a quantum computer — an exponential speedup. Now take unstructured search over one billion records: classically that's up to one billion checks in the worst case, but Grover's algorithm needs only floor of pi over four times the square root of one billion, which comes out to exactly 24,836 queries — a huge, real, but only quadratic speedup.

Two mistakes show up constantly. First, confusing NP with slow to solve — NP is defined by fast verification, and a problem can be in both NP and P at once, like sorting, which is in P and needs no quantum help at all, since O of n log n already beats anything quantum search could offer. Second, assuming any quantum speedup must be exponential — most known speedups, including the famous general-purpose one, Grover's algorithm, are only quadratic, which is exactly why TSP-decision stays NP-complete and exponential even with Grover's help.
Chapter 2 moves from classifying problems to building the actual machinery: the classical discrete Fourier transform, the tool the quantum Fourier transform is built from.
